dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: Each element is first included, then excluded, and subsets are recorded only at the leaves. 'Include' branches run first, so the full set comes first and the empty set last, which is why there's a trailing comma: 2^3 = 8 results. The ordering ,1,2,3,… comes from a BFS-style or bitmask enumeration.

res stores four references to the same path array, and after backtracking that array is empty, so every entry prints []. This is the most common backtracking bug. Push a snapshot instead: res.push([...path]). The count is still 4: [], [0], [0,1], [1].

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: In the choose / explore / un-choose template, why must you undo the choice (e.g. path.pop()) after the recursive call?
options: Because JavaScript arrays can't grow past the recursion depth
To free memory immediately
Because the path is shared, mutable state; undoing restores it so the next sibling branch starts from the same prefix
To prevent the recursion from running forever
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: All branches share one path array or used-set for efficiency. If you don't undo, a sibling branch inherits elements from the previous branch and produces wrong combinations. The alternative is to copy the state per call (immutable), which costs more memory.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: 'Permutations II' must generate unique permutations of [1, 1, 2]. After sorting, which skip condition prevents duplicates?
options: Skip i if nums[i] === nums[i + 1]
Skip i if used[i], or if i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]
Skip i if the path already contains nums[i]
Skip i if i > start
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: Equal values must be used in a fixed order: the second 1 can only be placed if the first 1 is already in the path. That rule blocks identical permutations that differ only in which copy came first. Checking whether the path contains the value would never allow both 1s.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: What's the time complexity of generating all permutations of n distinct elements, copying each one into the result?
options: O(n · n!)
O(n!) with no extra factor
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: There are n! permutations, and copying each one costs O(n), so the output alone is O(n · n!). O(2^n) counts subsets, a different problem. Saying O(n!) drops the copy cost, which interviewers usually expect you to mention.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: In N-Queens, how do you check in O(1) whether placing a queen at (r, c) is safe?
options: Keep a set of used rows only
Check only the cell directly above
Scan the whole board each time
Keep sets of used columns, of r - c (one diagonal direction) and of r + c (the other); a square is safe if none contains its value
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: Placing one queen per row handles rows. Cells on the same diagonal share r - c, and cells on the same anti-diagonal share r + c. Three sets make each check O(1) instead of an O(n) scan, and you must remove the entries when backtracking.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: Combination Sum (each candidate can be reused) returns both [2,3,2] and [3,2,2] as separate answers. What's the bug?
options: The target check is <= instead of ===
Candidates weren't sorted
Each recursive call loops from index 0 instead of from the current index, so the same multiset is built in different orders
The recursion uses i + 1, which forbids reuse
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: To produce combinations rather than permutations, pass a start index and loop from it: bt(i, remaining - c[i]) allows reuse while never going back to earlier candidates. Sorting helps pruning but doesn't prevent reorderings. Using i + 1 would forbid reuse, a different bug.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: For backtracking over positive integer candidates (as in Combination Sum), which pruning techniques are valid? Select all that apply.
options: Sorting is required for correctness in every backtracking problem
Sort the candidates and break out of the loop once a candidate exceeds the remaining target
Skip a candidate equal to the previous one at the same depth when the input has duplicates
Check constraints before recursing, rather than at the leaf
Memoize on the current path's contents to reduce the number of permutations that must be output
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: Breaking early works because the candidates are sorted and positive, so every later one is also too big. Same-depth duplicate skipping and early constraint checks cut whole subtrees. When you must output every permutation, memoization can't reduce the output size, and sorting is only needed by some prunings.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: Which problems are typically solved with backtracking? Select all that apply.
options: Generate all valid parentheses strings of n pairs
Word Search (does a word exist as a path in a letter grid?)
Fewest moves in an unweighted grid
Length of the longest common subsequence
Sudoku solver
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: Each of the first three builds a candidate step by step and abandons it as soon as a constraint fails. Fewest moves is a BFS problem, and LCS length has overlapping subproblems that DP solves in O(nm), where backtracking would be exponential.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: Generate Parentheses can prune by adding ')' only when the number of ')' placed so far is less than the number of '('.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: True. Together with adding '(' only while fewer than n have been placed, this guarantees every prefix is valid, so the recursion never builds an invalid string. The number of results is the n-th Catalan number.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.prompt: With good pruning, a backtracking algorithm is guaranteed to run in polynomial time.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:0.explanation: False. Pruning shrinks the search tree in practice, but the worst case usually stays exponential (N-Queens, Sudoku, subset sum). And if the problem asks you to list all solutions, the output itself can be exponential in size.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: A road network has 100,000 intersections and 250,000 roads. Which representation fits best?
options: An edge list scanned on every neighbour lookup
A matrix of booleans packed into a string
Adjacency matrix: 10^10 cells
Adjacency list (e.g. Map from node to neighbour array): O(V + E) memory
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: The graph is sparse (E is far smaller than V^2), so an adjacency list stores only the real edges, about 350k entries, and iterates a node's neighbours in O(degree). A matrix would need 10^10 cells. Scanning an edge list makes every neighbour lookup O(E).

A Map iterates keys in insertion order: a, b, c, d. c's neighbours are added in edge order: b (from b-c), a (from a-c), d (from c-d). size counts nodes (4), not directed entries; each undirected edge appears in two lists, so the lists contain 8 entries in total.

fill([]) puts the same array object in every slot, so pushing to g[0] changes all of them. Use Array.from({ length: n }, () => []) to get independent arrays. This bug silently connects every node to every neighbour.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: Why is a Map often preferable to a plain object for an adjacency list keyed by node id?
options: Maps sort their keys automatically
Maps are always faster for every operation
Map keeps key types (1 and '1' are different keys), has no inherited prototype keys, and has an O(1) size property
Objects can't hold arrays as values
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: Object keys are converted to strings, and integer-like keys are reordered ahead of the others. Maps keep keys as given (numbers, objects), iterate in insertion order and avoid prototype keys like 'constructor'. Maps don't sort, and objects can hold arrays fine.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: Your algorithm frequently asks 'is there an edge u to v?' on a large sparse graph stored as a Map of arrays. What change makes that check O(1) on average?
options: Sort each neighbour array and binary search, which is O(1)
Store neighbours in a Set per node (Map<node, Set<node>>)
Convert to an adjacency matrix regardless of size
Cache the result of the last query
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: Set.has is O(1) on average, compared with Array.includes at O(degree). A binary search is O(log degree), not O(1). A matrix gives O(1) but needs O(V^2) memory, which a large sparse graph can't afford.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: A grid BFS stores visited cells with `visited.add([r, c])` and checks `visited.has([nr, nc])`, but it never terminates on some inputs. Why?
options: Arrays are compared by reference, so each new [r, c] literal is a different key and has() is always false; use a string like `${r},${c}` or a number like r * cols + c
The Set grows past its maximum size
has() is O(n), which looks like an infinite loop
Sets can't store arrays
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: Set and Map use SameValueZero equality, which for objects means identity. Two different [1,2] arrays are different keys, so no cell ever counts as visited and cells get revisited endlessly. Encoding the coordinates as a primitive fixes it.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: Dijkstra on an undirected road map returns Infinity for some towns that are clearly reachable. The adjacency list is built with `g.get(u).push([v, w])` for each road. What's the most likely bug?
options: Weights must be integers
The priority queue should be a max-heap
Dijkstra doesn't support undirected graphs
Each road was added in one direction only; undirected edges must also push [u, w] into v's list
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: Pushing only u to v makes the graph directed, so a town reachable only by traversing some road from v to u looks unreachable. Undirected edges must be stored in both lists. Dijkstra works on undirected graphs with non-negative weights.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: When is an adjacency matrix preferable to an adjacency list? Select all that apply.
options: A sparse graph with 10^6 vertices
Iterating the neighbours of low-degree nodes quickly
Dense graphs where E is close to V^2
Small V where O(1) edge-existence checks matter
Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest paths, which works over a V × V table anyway
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: A matrix costs O(V^2) memory, which is reasonable when the graph is dense or small and buys O(1) edge checks. Floyd-Warshall needs a V × V table anyway. For 10^6 vertices it would need about 10^12 cells, and finding a node's neighbours means scanning a whole row, O(V).

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: You build an adjacency list for nodes 0..n-1 from an edge list. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Array.from({ length: n }, () => []) creates an independent array per node
Isolated nodes keep empty lists and must still be visited when counting connected components
For a directed edge u to v, only g[u] gets v
In an undirected graph, the sum of all list lengths equals E
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: The factory callback creates a fresh array each time. Components are counted by looping over all n nodes, so isolated nodes count as components of size 1. A directed edge belongs in one list only. In an undirected graph each edge appears in two lists, so the total is 2E.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: Iterating a Map with for...of visits its entries in the order the keys were first inserted.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: True. Maps guarantee insertion order, and re-setting an existing key doesn't move it. That makes graph traversals over a Map deterministic. Plain objects instead put integer-like keys first, in numeric order.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.prompt: For an undirected graph stored as adjacency lists, the total length of all the lists equals the number of edges E.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:1.explanation: False. Each undirected edge {u, v} appears in both u's list and v's list, so the total is 2E (the handshake lemma: the degrees sum to 2E). For a directed graph the total is E.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: The islands are the 2×2 block at the top left, the single cell (1,3), the single cell (2,2), and the pair (3,3)-(3,4). (1,3) and (2,2) touch only diagonally, and the DFS moves in 4 directions only, so they're separate islands. With diagonal moves, (1,3), (2,2) and the pair would merge into one island, giving 2.

The wall at (1,1) forces the path down the left column and along the bottom row: (2,2) is 4 steps away and (1,2) is 5, reached by stepping up from (2,2). (0,2) is a wall and stays -1. BFS assigns each cell its shortest distance the first time it reaches it.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: In BFS, why mark a node as visited when it's enqueued rather than when it's dequeued?
options: Marking at enqueue stops the same node from being added to the queue several times by different neighbours, which wastes time and memory
Marking at enqueue makes BFS behave like DFS
It doesn't matter in any case
Marking at dequeue gives wrong distances
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: If you mark only when dequeuing, a node with many already-discovered neighbours can be enqueued once per neighbour, so the queue can grow towards O(E) duplicates. Distances stay correct for unweighted BFS, but you lose the clean O(V) queue bound.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: 'Rotting oranges': every minute, rotten oranges rot their 4 neighbours. How do you compute the time until all oranges are rotten?
options: DFS from the first fresh orange
Run Dijkstra from the top-left cell
Run a BFS from each rotten orange separately and take the maximum
Multi-source BFS: put all rotten oranges in the queue at time 0 and expand level by level
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: Starting the BFS from all sources at once gives each cell its distance to the nearest rotten orange in one O(R·C) pass. Separate BFS runs cost O(k·R·C) and still need a minimum per cell, not a maximum. If any fresh orange is never reached, the answer is -1.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: A recursive flood fill works on small tests but crashes in Node on a 1000×1000 grid that is all land. What's the cause and fix?
options: JS strings can't be mutated; convert rows to arrays
The grid is too large for memory; use a Uint8Array
The recursion depth can reach about 10^6 and overflow the call stack; use an explicit stack or a BFS queue
Recursion visits cells twice; add a visited set
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: DFS on a snake-like or full grid can go about R·C calls deep, and V8's stack overflows after roughly 10k calls (depending on frame size) with a RangeError. An iterative version keeps the stack on the heap. The grid itself (10^6 cells) fits easily in memory.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: Edges have weight 0 or 1 only. What's the most efficient shortest-path approach?
options: Plain BFS, ignoring weights
0-1 BFS with a deque: push the neighbour to the front for a 0-weight edge and to the back for a 1-weight edge, giving O(V + E)
Bellman-Ford
DFS with memoization
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: The deque keeps nodes in non-decreasing distance order without a heap, so this is Dijkstra in O(V + E). Plain BFS treats 0-weight edges as cost 1 and gets wrong answers. Bellman-Ford is O(VE).

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: 'Shortest path in a grid with obstacle elimination' lets you remove up to k obstacles. Why is a visited[r][c] array alone wrong?
options: Reaching a cell with more eliminations left is a different, better state; marking the cell visited on the first arrival can block a path that arrives later with more eliminations remaining
BFS can't handle obstacles
visited should be cleared after each level
It uses too much memory
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: The BFS state is (r, c, remaining eliminations). Track visited per state, or keep the best remaining count per cell and revisit only if the new arrival has more left. Otherwise an early arrival that has used up its eliminations hides a better route.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: Which cycle-detection approaches are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Undirected graph: union-find, reporting a cycle when an edge joins two nodes already in the same set
Directed graph: report a cycle whenever DFS reaches any already-visited node
Undirected graph: DFS that reports a cycle when it finds a visited neighbour other than the parent it came from
Directed graph: DFS with three states (unvisited, on the current path, done), reporting a cycle on reaching a node that's on the current path
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: In a directed graph, reaching a node that's already finished (a cross or forward edge) is not a cycle; only a back edge to a node on the current path is. The parent check, the three-state DFS and union-find are the standard correct methods.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: Which tasks need BFS (rather than plain DFS) to get the answer directly? Select all that apply.
options: Distance from every cell to its nearest 0 in a binary matrix
Fewest moves to reach the exit of an unweighted maze
Word Ladder: the minimum number of transformations
Counting connected components
Checking whether any path exists between two nodes
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: Minimum steps in an unweighted graph come from BFS's level-by-level order, and 'distance to nearest 0' is a multi-source BFS. Component counting and plain reachability only need every reachable node visited, so DFS works equally well.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: Flood fill on a grid of V cells runs in O(V) time when each cell is marked visited the first time it's reached.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: True. Each cell is processed at most once and checks a constant 4 (or 8) neighbours, so the total is O(V). Without marking, cells get revisited, the work can blow up, and on cyclic regions the fill never terminates.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.prompt: In a DFS over an undirected graph, finding an already-visited neighbour always means there is a cycle.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:2.explanation: False. In an undirected graph, the node you just came from is always a visited neighbour, because the edge is stored in both directions. A cycle exists only if a visited neighbour other than the parent is found. With parallel edges, track the edge id instead of the parent node.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: 0 is the only node with in-degree 0. Removing it frees 1 and 2, enqueued in adjacency order. 3 needs both 1 and 2 to be processed before its in-degree reaches 0. 0,2,1,3 is also a valid topological order, but this code's FIFO queue produces 0,1,2,3.

1 and 2 form a cycle, so after 0 is removed node 1 still has in-degree 1 (from 2) and never enters the queue. Node 3 depends on 2 and is stuck too. Only 0 is output. An output shorter than n is how Kahn's algorithm detects a cycle.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: In 'Course Schedule', when is it impossible to finish all courses?
options: When some course has more than two prerequisites
When the prerequisite graph contains a directed cycle
When the graph is disconnected
When a course has no prerequisites
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: A topological order exists if and only if the directed graph is acyclic. A cycle means courses wait on each other forever. A disconnected graph is fine: each part is ordered independently. The number of prerequisites per course doesn't matter.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: In DFS-based topological sort, when is a node added to the output, and what's done with the output at the end?
options: After all its descendants are finished (post-order); reverse the list at the end
When its in-degree becomes 0; output as is
Before visiting its neighbours; reverse the list at the end
When it's first visited; output as is
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: A node finishes only after everything reachable from it has finished, so its dependents are already in the list. Reversing the finish order puts every node before its dependents. Recording nodes on first visit (preorder) can place a node before one of its prerequisites.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means 'take b before a'. A solution builds edges a to b and prints an order where courses appear before their prerequisites. What's wrong?
options: The queue should be a stack
In-degrees should be counted on the source node
Kahn's algorithm can't handle this input format
The edges are reversed; they should go b to a (prerequisite to dependent), otherwise the topological order comes out backwards
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: Edges must point from what comes first to what depends on it. With reversed edges the algorithm still detects cycles correctly, since reversing every edge keeps cycles, but the order is backwards. Using a stack instead of a queue gives another valid order, not a fix.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: You need the lexicographically smallest valid topological order of a DAG with numbered nodes. What change to Kahn's algorithm achieves it?
options: Process nodes in reverse numeric order
Sort the final output
Replace the FIFO queue with a min-heap, so the smallest available node is taken each time: O((V + E) log V)
Run DFS from the smallest node first
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: At each step, taking the smallest node whose prerequisites are all done is the greedy choice that gives the smallest sequence. Sorting the final output breaks the dependency order. Running DFS from the smallest node doesn't guarantee the smallest overall sequence.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: In 'Alien Dictionary', the word list contains 'abc' immediately followed by 'ab'. What should the algorithm do?
options: Add the edge c to b
Ignore the pair because no characters differ
Return '' (invalid input), because a longer word can't come before its own prefix in a sorted dictionary
Swap the two words and continue
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: Comparing adjacent words gives no differing character, yet the longer word comes first, which no letter ordering allows. Skipping the pair silently accepts invalid input, and it's a classic hidden test case. When adjacent words do differ, the first differing character pair gives one edge.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: Which tasks are solved by topological sorting? Select all that apply.
options: Choosing an install order for packages with dependencies
Deciding the order to recompute spreadsheet cells after an edit
Shortest paths in an undirected weighted graph
Detecting a cycle in an undirected graph via in-degrees
Ordering build steps or jobs that depend on each other
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: Dependency graphs with directed 'must come before' edges are exactly what topological sort orders. Undirected shortest paths need Dijkstra, and in-degree is a directed-graph idea; undirected cycles are found with DFS (skipping the parent) or union-find.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: 'Parallel courses': any number of courses can be taken per semester once their prerequisites are done. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A DFS topological sort without an 'on the current path' state can silently produce an order on a cyclic graph
Kahn's algorithm requires an undirected graph
The minimum number of semesters equals the number of vertices on the longest path in the DAG
Running Kahn's algorithm level by level (one BFS layer per semester) gives that number
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: Each layer of Kahn's BFS is one semester, and the number of layers equals the longest dependency chain. A plain visited-set DFS can't distinguish back edges, so it outputs an order even when a cycle exists. Kahn's algorithm works on directed graphs; in-degree has no meaning for undirected ones.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: A DAG can have more than one valid topological order.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: True. Whenever two nodes don't depend on each other, either can come first. In the diamond 0 to {1, 2} to 3, both 0,1,2,3 and 0,2,1,3 are valid. The order is unique only if consecutive nodes in it are always joined by an edge (a Hamiltonian path).

dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.prompt: DFS-based topological sort outputs nodes in the order they're first discovered (preorder).
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:3.explanation: False. It uses reverse post-order, the order in which nodes finish, reversed. Preorder can list a node before one of its prerequisites when DFS reaches it through another branch. For edges A to C, B to C and B to A, DFS from A gives preorder A, C, B, but B must come before A.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: The first three unions merge different sets: {0,1,2} and {3,4}, with 5 alone. union(0, 2) finds that both have the same root and returns false; in 'redundant connection' that edge is the one closing a cycle. Each successful union removes one component: 6 - 3 = 3.

The chain is 4 to 3 to 2 to 1 to 0. Recursive path compression points every node on the path directly at the root as the recursion returns, not just the starting node. Later finds on any of them take one hop.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: 'Redundant connection': a tree with one extra edge is given as an edge list. How does union-find identify the extra edge?
options: The edge whose endpoints are both leaves
The edge whose endpoints have the highest combined rank
Process the edges in order; the first edge whose endpoints already have the same root closes a cycle
The edge that's processed last
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: If find(u) === find(v), u and v are already connected, so adding the edge creates a cycle. Processing in input order returns the cycle edge that appears last in the input, which is what the problem asks for. Ranks and leaves are irrelevant here.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: With both path compression and union by rank (or size), what's the amortized cost per operation?
options: O(log n)
O(α(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, at most about 4 for any practical n
O(1) worst case for every operation
O(√n)
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: Tarjan's analysis gives O(α(n)) amortized, which is effectively constant. It isn't O(1) worst case: a single find before compression can still traverse a path of length O(log n) (with union by rank). Either optimization alone gives O(log n).

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: Why use union by rank or size, rather than always attaching the first root under the second?
options: Without it, a sequence of unions can build a chain of height O(n), making find O(n) until path compression flattens it
It's needed to count components
It lets union-find support deleting an edge
It makes union return the right boolean
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: Attaching the smaller or shallower tree under the larger keeps the height O(log n), because a node's depth grows only when its tree at least doubles in size. Naive unions like union(1,0), union(2,1), … build a long chain. Component counting works either way.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: In a graph where edges are only ever removed, you must answer 'are u and v connected?' after each removal. Why is plain union-find awkward, and what's the common trick?
options: Union-find is too slow; use a heap
Union-find only works on trees
Union-find can't store edges; use BFS each time
Union-find can't split sets; process the operations offline in reverse, so removals become additions (unions), and answer the queries backwards
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: Union-find supports merging but not splitting. If all operations are known in advance, reversing time turns deletions into unions, which it handles well. Running BFS after each deletion costs O(V + E) per query, which is usually too slow.

options: find must be called after the assignment
It should return true when the roots are equal
It re-parents node a instead of a's root, so a's old set isn't merged and a is detached from it
It should set parent[b] = a
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: Union must link the roots: parent[find(a)] = find(b). Setting parent[a] moves only a into b's tree, while the rest of a's set keeps its old root, so connectivity becomes wrong. Swapping a and b has the same problem.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: Which problems fit union-find? Select all that apply.
options: Number of connected components as edges arrive one by one
Kruskal's minimum spanning tree
Detecting the redundant edge in an undirected graph
Shortest path in an unweighted graph
Topological ordering of a DAG
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: Union-find answers connectivity questions under merges, which covers incremental components, Kruskal's 'would this edge form a cycle?' check and redundant edges. It records which set a node belongs to, not distances or directions, so shortest paths and topological order need BFS or DFS.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: Which statements about union-find complexity are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Union by rank alone keeps tree height O(log n), so find is O(log n) worst case
Using both gives O(α(n)) amortized
With path compression, every find is O(1) worst case
Path compression alone gives O(log n) amortized per operation
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: Each optimization alone gives logarithmic bounds, and together they give the inverse-Ackermann bound. Compression is amortized: the first find on a long path still walks the whole path, then flattens it for later calls.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: Union-find can tell you whether two nodes are connected, but it can't by itself return the path between them.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: True. The parent pointers form trees that have nothing to do with the graph's actual edges, especially after path compression. To get a path you need BFS or DFS on the adjacency list.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.prompt: Union by rank requires rank to equal each tree's exact height, so ranks must be recomputed whenever path compression shortens a tree.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:4.explanation: False. Rank is only an upper bound on height. Path compression lowers actual heights but leaves ranks alone, and the O(α(n)) analysis assumes exactly that. Recomputing heights would cost extra and gain nothing. Union by size is an equivalent alternative.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: A to C costs 1, and A to C to B costs 3, which beats the direct 4. Then B to D costs 3 + 1 = 4, which beats C to D at 6. The stale [4, 'B'] entry is skipped by the d > dist[u] check (lazy deletion). The sorted array stands in for a heap here.

Each edge is [weight, u, v]. Kruskal takes them in weight order: 1 (0-1), 2 (2-3), 3 (1-2, joining the two parts), then skips 4 and 5 because they would form cycles. A spanning tree on 4 nodes always has V - 1 = 3 edges, here with total weight 6.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm return wrong answers when some edge weights are negative?
options: It always runs forever on negative edges
Negative weights make the graph disconnected
The heap can't store negative numbers
It finalizes a node when it's popped, assuming no shorter path can appear later, but a later negative edge can make a shorter path to an already-settled node
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: Dijkstra's correctness relies on path costs never decreasing as edges are added, which negative edges break. A node popped with distance 5 might later be reachable for 3 through a negative edge. Without a negative cycle it doesn't loop forever; it just returns wrong distances.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle reachable from the source?
options: By detecting that the priority queue grows past V entries
By checking for any negative edge weight
After V - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge, it runs one more round; if any distance still decreases, a negative cycle exists
By running Dijkstra twice and comparing
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: A shortest simple path has at most V - 1 edges, so V - 1 rounds are enough when no negative cycle exists. If a V-th round still improves something, some path keeps getting cheaper, which means a negative cycle. Negative edges alone are allowed. Total time O(V·E).

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: What's the time complexity of Dijkstra with a binary heap and lazy deletion, on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
options: O((V + E) log V)
O(V · E)
O(E)
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: Each edge can push one heap entry and each push or pop costs O(log E), which is O(log V) since E ≤ V^2. That gives O((V + E) log V). O(V^2) is the array-based version without a heap, which is better only for very dense graphs. O(V·E) is Bellman-Ford.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: 'Cheapest flights within K stops' is solved with Bellman-Ford limited to K + 1 rounds. Why does each round relax from a copy of the previous round's distances?
options: So each round extends paths by at most one edge; relaxing in place could chain several edges in one round and exceed the stop limit
Because JS arrays can't be updated during iteration
To detect negative cycles
To avoid mutating the input
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: Relaxing in place can use a distance updated earlier in the same round, chaining two or more flights into one round. Reading from the previous round's snapshot caps round i at i edges. Plain Dijkstra on cost alone ignores the stop limit too.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: You need a minimum spanning tree for a dense graph (E close to V^2) given as an adjacency matrix with V = 5,000. Which choice is most natural?
options: Bellman-Ford
BFS spanning tree
Kruskal, because sorting E ≈ 25 million edges is cheap
Prim's O(V^2) array version: no heap, scanning for the closest vertex each step, which suits a matrix
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: Array-based Prim does V steps of an O(V) scan, about 25 million operations, without building or sorting an edge list. Kruskal must sort about 25M edges, O(E log E), which is slower. A BFS tree ignores weights, and Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths, not spanning trees.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: Which statements about minimum spanning trees are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An MST of a connected graph with V nodes has V edges
If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique
An MST minimizes total edge weight, but the MST path between two nodes isn't necessarily their shortest path
Cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST
Kruskal's algorithm finds minimum spanning arborescences in directed graphs
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: The cut property justifies both Prim and Kruskal, and distinct weights make the MST unique. Minimizing total weight doesn't minimize each pairwise distance. Directed graphs need Chu-Liu/Edmonds, and a spanning tree has exactly V - 1 edges.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: Which algorithm-to-scenario pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Non-negative weights, single source: Dijkstra
Negative edge weights, no negative cycle: Bellman-Ford
All-pairs shortest paths on a small dense graph: Floyd-Warshall
Negative edge weights: Dijkstra with lazy deletion
Unweighted shortest path: BFS
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: BFS handles unit weights, Dijkstra non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford negative edges (and detects negative cycles), and Floyd-Warshall runs in O(V^3) for all pairs. Lazy deletion is only a heap trick; it doesn't fix Dijkstra's assumption that weights are non-negative.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm computes correct shortest paths when edge weights are zero or positive.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: True. Zero-weight edges are allowed: the algorithm only needs weights to be non-negative, so path costs never decrease as you extend a path. That's what makes finalizing the smallest-distance node safe. Negative edges break this.

dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.prompt: Prim's and Dijkstra's algorithms use the same priority key: a vertex's total distance from the start node.
options: True
False
dsa-backtracking-graphs:5.explanation: False. The code looks almost the same, but Prim keys each vertex by the weight of the single cheapest edge connecting it to the current tree, while Dijkstra keys it by the total path distance from the source. Mixing the two up is a common interview mistake.
